intro_html:
Florida has no plug-in solar law, and its well-known solar rights statute stops short of the balcony. Section 163.04 of the Florida Statutes bars ordinances, deed restrictions, covenants and similar agreements that prohibit “solar collectors, clotheslines, or other energy devices based on renewable resources”, and says a property owner may not be denied permission to install one within the boundaries of a condominium unit. Its final sentence then reads: “This section shall not apply to patio railings in condominiums, cooperatives, or apartments.” A panel on a condo, co-op or apartment railing is the case it expressly leaves out. Vermont’s statute carried the same sentence until 2026, when it was amended to except plug-in devices; Florida’s has not been. The statute also protects property owners, not tenants.

Grid connection is the other gate. State law requires investor-owned utilities such as FPL, under Public Service Commission rules, and municipal utilities and cooperatives, under their own boards, to offer a standardized interconnection agreement for customer-owned renewable generation. Jacksonville’s utility, JEA, is municipal: customers who want to connect a renewable generation system to its grid must apply to its Distributed Generation Program, and JEA asks them to review its interconnection requirements before installing. Nothing in Florida law exempts a small plug-in device from that process, and balco.nyc’s figures below assume none of its output is sold.

faq: Does Florida's Solar Rights Act protect a balcony solar panel in a condo?

No. Section 163.04 of the Florida Statutes protects solar collectors and other renewable energy devices from deed restrictions and association bans, including within the boundaries of a condominium unit, but states that it does not apply to patio railings in condominiums, cooperatives, or apartments.
